det3 June-15 build · X view · cosmic bench June 2026 · raw DREAM ADC

The X asymmetry is real and in the raw ADC: every June-built board carries a smooth X field of unequal neighbours, most likely from how its resistive stripes sit over the pads

On det3’s June-15 build the channel above the peak is the bigger neighbour in 84 % of events; every other board and view through the same code sits at 50 %. Simulated stripe registration gives the right shape at 1/3–2/3 of the size; the production reconstruction carries the field, and an opt-in correction now exists.

1

Details

This deck answers one question: is the det3 X left/right neighbour asymmetry (NB_ASYM.md) a real detector effect, or something the analysis made? It starts from the most basic observable there is and builds up.

Everything here was recomputed from the decoded DREAM files with a new extractor, raw_asym.py, that shares no code with the earlier analysis (no FeuReader, no strip map, no common-mode subtraction). The earlier copy survey is used only where noted.

Short answer: yes, it is real, it is a copy of the peak channel’s own pulse into its upper channel neighbour, it follows the board (not the FEU slot, not the view), it is strongest in the middle of the board, and it changes with drift field. Its cause is not established.

What is measured: a cosmic, a few pads, three channels

Hover the dotted terms and any data point for definitions, counts and sources.

2

Details

A cosmic muon ionises the ~27 mm drift gap; electrons drift to the mesh, avalanche in the 150 µm gap, and induce signal on the readout pads under the resistive layer. The pads form a checkerboard: every other pad belongs to an X channel, the others to a Y channel (gerbers: 131 072 stubs each). Each pad reaches its channel’s bus line through a via and a 390 µm stub, and every stub of a layer points the same way, so each bus runs under the inter-pad gap on one side of its pads. That is the only built-in left/right asymmetry of the board we know of; slide 18 asks how large an effect it can make.

The readout: 512 channels per view, 64-channel connectors and DREAM chips, 32 samples of 60 ns per channel per trigger. These runs had no zero suppression, no on-board pedestal and no common-noise subtraction (run_config dream_daq_info).

Throughout: p is the channel with the largest pulse; p−1 and p+1 are its neighbours in DAQ channel number. With the connector-inverted wiring of all these runs, channel p+1 sits at the lower strip position.

Grey: symmetric by construction. Red: the one built-in asymmetry. Gold: places an analysis or readout artefact could hide.

3

Details

Your prior is the right one: nothing in the physics of a micromegas prefers one side. Cosmics arrive from both sides, diffusion and the avalanche are isotropic, and the resistive-strip/pad beat averages to zero over the board (NB_ASYM §1: peak rank mod 40 shows no modulation, sine amplitude 0.020 ± 0.024).

So a left/right difference has to come either from the hardware layout (the bus traces are one-sided), from the readout (adjacent pins, the order the ADC reads channels), or from the analysis. The deck tests each in turn and comes back to this chain at the end with a verdict per box.

5

Details

Every step is symmetric between p−1 and p+1: a per-channel constant, an argmax over channels, and two array lookups. A per-channel gain difference cannot create a net asymmetry either, because p runs over all channels and each channel is p−1 for one peak and p+1 for another.

The cuts act on the peak channel only and never look at the neighbours, except the isolation (no other channel over 5σ beyond p ± 3), which is symmetric.

Hot channels: a channel that fires on noise produces “events” with p always the same channel, so its two fixed neighbours decide the left/right answer. The veto removes a channel that is the peak more than six times the median rate of the channels that ever are. On det3 June X it removes channel 492 (6-23/24 runs).

Sources: raw_asym.py, asym_lib.py

Which neighbour is bigger? A coin flip, except det3 X

Fraction of clean events where channel p+1 has a larger pulse than p−1 · every board and view, same code

6

Details

This is the simplest observable I can think of: for each event, is the right neighbour (channel p+1) bigger than the left (p−1)? It needs no calibration, no model and no strip map. A detector with no left/right preference gives 50 % within the binomial error.

det3’s June-15 build in X is far off (both runs, on two different FEUs); its Y view, read at the same time, is at 50 %. The May build of det3, read through the same FEU 3, is at 50 %. det4 and det7 X (built in Stephan’s June-22 batch) sit a few % high. The weekend det3 run is lower because its neighbours are wider (a copy of the same absolute size changes the ranking less).

The excess is a 23 % copy of the peak’s own pulse

det3 June-15 X, 6-24 long run · samples where the peak pulse is above 20 % of its maximum

9

Details

If the extra charge on p+1 were real induced charge from a displaced cloud, or a crosstalk through a capacitor (which differentiates), it would have its own shape and timing. Instead the mean difference (p+1) − (p−1) is the peak channel’s own pulse times a constant, sample by sample, including the long tail.

NB_ASYM §1 fitted d = a·c + b·dc/dt on the earlier tagged dumps: b ≈ 0, residual rms 0.002–0.010.

So the cleanest description is: channel p+1 receives a fixed fraction of whatever channel p carries, at the same time. The next slide tests that “copy” description on the second neighbours.

Sources: asym_lib.load

10

Details

The copy model has one parameter. Undoing it runs upward through the channel window: x′(n+1) = x(n+1) − a·x′(n). Fitting a so that the first neighbours balance gives a = 0.192. The second neighbours were not used in the fit; raw they are p−2 0.0236 vs p+2 0.0347, after undoing 0.0224 vs 0.0086.

NB_ASYM §1 found the same on the tagged dumps (a from ±1 and from ±2 agree on every run: 0.085/0.085, 0.145/0.142, 0.196/0.167), and uncopy.py closes the full-FEU version (6-22: ±1 0.153 → 0.005).

In-phase content α_k = Σ_t x_k(t)·x_p(t) / Σ_t x_p(t)²: the part of channel p+k shaped like the peak pulse.

Sources: asym_lib.fit_copy, asym_lib.uncopy, ../uncopy.py

The noise isn’t copied: it is not the electronics

Correlation between channel n and n+d on triggers with nothing above 5σ in the chip · 6-24 long run

det3 June-15 X

… with a 0.15 copy injected

det3 June-15 Y

det3 May X

The signal is copied, the noise is not. A copy made in the cable, the FEU or the ADC would copy both.

So the extra charge is induced before the preamplifier input: on the detector, or between its pads and the connector.

11

Details

Every DREAM channel has its own preamplifier noise. If anything after the input (shaper, multiplexer, ADC settling, a cable between FEU stages) added a × channel n to channel n+1, the noise would be copied too, and the correlation between neighbours (d = 1) would jump relative to d = 2. Injecting x(n+1) += 0.15 x(n) into these same quiet samples shows the size of that jump (dashed).

The measured X correlation has no d = 1 spike, the same as its Y view and as the May build (same FEU 3, no copy). The correlations themselves are common-mode residue; their level differs between boards and runs, so compare the shape (d = 1 vs d = 2), not the level.

Caveat: noise injected at the preamp input (its series noise) appears on the input node; coupling between input lines could carry some of it. So this test excludes the FEU chain, not a coupling on the input traces or connector. That one is addressed by “follows the board” (next slide) and by the field dependence (slide 17).

NB_ASYM had the same result with the older dumps (+0.03/−0.03/−0.02 vs +0.06…0.12 for an injected 0.1 copy).

Sources: raw_asym.py (corr_cm, corr_inj), ../noise_corr.py

It follows the board, not the FEU slot

The copy follows the board and its X view, not the readout slot.

12

Details

FEU 3 read det3’s May build (May 6), det6 (June 26) and det3’s June-15 build (June 22–24): only the last copies. det3’s June-15 build was moved to FEU 7 for the June 27–28 runs and still copies. Its Y view, read in the same triggers on FEU 4 or 8, never does.

What this does not settle: whether det3’s X cable or adapter travelled with the board between slots. If one specific cable did, it could still be the culprit. The field dependence (slide 17) argues against a cable.

Also the May and June-15 “det3” builds may not be the same PCB (the run configs say “Bulked 5-5-26” and “Bulked by Stephan June 15”). If they are the same PCB, the copy appeared with the re-bulking.

Sources: asym_lib.load, run_config.json dream_feus

13

Details

Each DREAM chip reads 64 adjacent X channels, about 50 mm of the board. The copy is ~0.1 at the two ends (chips 0, 1, 7) and 0.2–0.3 in chips 2–5, with the same shape on every run and at both drift fields. Chip order follows the board’s x position (the connectors sit in order along the edge).

This matters for the cause. A layout feature of the PCB (the bus traces, the connector pin order) repeats identically for every channel and every chip, so it would give a flat profile. A profile that peaks in the middle points to something that varies over the board’s area: the mesh or drift-gap geometry (a bowed mesh or cathode changes the local field), the bulk (lamination, pillars, coverlay thickness, curing), or moisture.

Right: matched X and Y events (same trigger) binned by both coordinates, so the dependence on y (along the X strips) can be seen too. Grey cells have fewer than 25 events.

Sources: asym_lib.load, raw_asym.py t622L_x t623L_x t623L_y t627d100_x t627d1100_x d3wk_x

14

Details

A threshold, saturation or a non-linear ADC effect would make the copy depend on the pulse height. It is flat within errors from 200 to 3500 ADC: a linear coupling.

NB_ASYM also found it flat in track angle (a real tilt gives −0.0085 per degree on det2; det3’s copy would need ~20°), flat in channel-within-connector and parity, and flat in the 39:40 resistive-strip beat phase.

Sources: asym_lib.load, ../nb_copy_vs_amp.py, ../nb_copy_vs_angle.py, ../nb_asym.py

A real trap: a hot channel faked a “turn-on” one evening

det3 June-15 X, 6-23 evening → 6-24 morning (same HV) · copy per data file, with and without the hot-channel veto

15

Details

The earlier survey (copy_survey.csv) showed det3’s copy at 0.035 at 19:29, 0.057 at 20:29 and 0.17 overnight, at unchanged HV, which looked like a slow turn-on. It is not. In the short run 3259 of 4493 “events” are channel 492 firing on noise (flat waveforms, no pulse); its two fixed neighbours decide the answer, and they happen to be nearly equal. As the run goes on, real cosmics outnumber it and the mean climbs to the true value.

With the pulse-shape cut and the hot-channel veto every file of the evening gives the same copy, and the per-chip profile of the longer run equals the long run’s.

This is exactly the kind of algorithm effect worth worrying about, and it shows the veto is needed before any time-dependence claim. The survey slides below use the raw re-extraction with the veto.

Sources: asym_lib.hot, raw_asym.py t623s_x t623l_x t623L_x

det3 X copy per sub-run · raw extraction, hot channels vetoed · board-centre chips only · colour: drift voltage

FEU 7 slot

17

Details

Each point is one sub-run of det3 X (an HV/drift-scan point or a long run) with at least 60 clean events in the board-centre chips 2–5; bars are the standard error. Centre chips only, because the copy is centre-peaked (~0.25 mid-board, ~0.1 at the edges) and several 6-22 high-mesh points have 70–90 % of their hits on chip 7: their board average reads low for a reason that has nothing to do with time. The tooltip has both numbers. Bold numbers: inverse-variance mean of each session (the 6-27 one mixes the drift scan with the 1000 V runs; its 1000 V runs alone are ≈ 0.10).

Reading it: 6-18 (first night, FEU 7, only chips 0–3 lit) 0.26. 6-19/20 (FEU 7, 7458 events, flat through all 8 files, no centre peak) 0.03. 6-22/23 (FEU 3, drift 1000 V) 0.16, flat through 12 h. 6-23/24 at drift 600 V 0.26, flat through 7 h. 6-25 drift 500 V 0.17. 6-27/28 (FEU 7, resist HV moved 3:3 → 3:4) 0.09–0.10 at 1000 V, rising to 0.21 at 100 V. 7-26 beam run_79 0.05–0.07 (Ar/iso 90/10, drift 700 V; older method on the whole board, and the same method gives −0.04 on det3 Y there, so treat it as ≲ 0.1). May build ≈ 0 throughout.

What it says: the copy is stable within a session (hours) and jumps between sessions (days). It is not a slow monotonic decay: it was large on the first night, near zero the next, back two days later. Drift field moves it (×1.6–2 from 1000 V to ≲ 600 V) but cannot explain 6-19, which ran at 1000 V like 6-22. The slot (FEU 3 vs 7) cannot either: 6-18 and 6-19 were both on FEU 7.

The one thing special about 6-19: it is the only run where det3’s drift channel (0:7 in that config) misbehaved, 4–9 µA spikes with the voltage sagging to 890–960 V in most sub-runs, against a flat 0.34 µA (the module’s own load) in every other run. Resist current was also high (2–4 µA at 500 V vs ~1 µA). A board that was discharging in the drift gap all night carried no copy. One coincidence, not a mechanism, but it fits a charge-on-a-surface picture (sparks neutralising it) better than any fixed coupling. Caveat: the 6-19 config swapped the HV channels between the two boards relative to 6-17; the other board that night (FEU 3) reads 0.08 ± 0.03 from 372 noisy events, so it is not a clean label swap, but a cabling mix-up that night is not excluded.

Missing: the 6-26 weekend scan (FEU 3) is empty on EOS; the 6-19 HV scan and long_run exist only as raw_daq_data (not decoded), so they could extend 6-19/20 if decoded.

Sources: raw survey, extra/d617_long_x.npz, extra/d619_longer_x.npz (EOS june_tests, raw_asym.py), hv_monitor.csv per sub-run, ../copy_survey.csv (beam)

Not constant: it rises as the drift field drops

det3 June-15 X · raw re-extraction, hot channels vetoed · colour: drift voltage (dark low, yellow high)

18

Details

Left: every bench sub-run of det3’s June-15 build in X, at its start time. It is highest on 6-22/24 (FEU 3) and lower on 6-27/28 (FEU 7). The step coincides with the slot change, so time and slot are confounded here; the drift scan on the right is within one slot and one evening.

Right: the 6-27 drift scan ran from 1100 V down to 100 V in time order; the copy rises as the field drops. The long run that started right after, at 1000 V, returns to the 1000 V value: the field dependence is reversible, not a drift in time.

Middle: the mesh HV scans are flat up to ~500 V. Above it most peaks rail (cut), the surviving samples are small and several hot channels are vetoed, so the points there are few and noisy; they are not evidence of a gain dependence.

Why this matters: a cable, a connector or the FEU cannot know the drift field. A detector-side effect can: the drift field sets the field just above the mesh and the electron transparency, and any charge sitting on insulating surfaces near the pads responds to it.

Sources: raw survey, ../copy_survey.csv (start times, HV)

Only charge over a Y pad is copied, on every board that has it

X and Y matched event by event; the pad type under the charge from the parity of the two peak channels

charge over an X pad

charge over a Y pad

det3 June-15: 0.22 over Y pads, 0.02 over X pads. det4 and det7 show the same split at a third of the size.

19

Details

Method: for each sub-run the X and Y dumps are matched by file index and eventId. In the checkerboard the parity of (peak X channel + peak Y channel) tells whether the charge sits over an X pad or a Y pad. Which parity is which is read from the data itself: the Y-pad class has the smaller Y ±1 share and the smaller A_x/A_y (det3 June-15: A_x/A_y 0.94 vs 1.10, Y share 0.65 vs 0.92).

Control: a forward model with the solved weighting fields and a symmetric geometry (fwd_parity.py) gives 0 in both classes, as mirror symmetry demands. Correction 10-20 (slide “Caution”): that only shows the classification makes no asymmetry from nothing. Applied to a plain channel copy, the peak selection does make a split (det2 + 0.3 → 0.20 / 0.05), so the contrast here is partly selection. det3 June-15 still differs from a plain copy (slide “Not a copy”).

Within the Y-pad class the copy is the same at every Y pad: flat in (X ch mod k, Y ch mod k) for k = 3, 4, 6 (the pillar grid is 6 pads) and 12 (χ²/ndf 1.0–1.6). So it is not the pillars. The 40-channel (ESL beat) check here used DAQ channels; redone with true columns on slide “Stripes”: still flat.

Reading: for a Y pad its left and right neighbours are X pads of the central X line and the pads above and below belong to the two X neighbours; the copy is an imbalance between those two, about 0.43/0.18 of the central instead of 0.31/0.31. For an X pad the X neighbours are diagonal and the direct signal dominates.

Sources: asym_more.py, fwd_parity.py, raw survey

It changes along one board axis only, and not with the local drift time

det3 June-15, Y-pad events, per 64-channel chip · three sessions

6-22/23, 1000 V, FEU 3

6-23/24, 600 V, FEU 3

6-27/28, 1000 V, FEU 7

With your orientation (X cards at the bottom, Y cards on the right) the Y-chip axis is top to bottom: the inlet-to-exhaust direction. The copy is flat along it.

20

Details

Left: along the X-chip axis the copy falls by a factor 2–3 from chips 1–3 to chip 7, in every session. Right: along the Y-chip axis it is flat within ~±0.03.

The local pulse width (a drift-time proxy, in the tooltips) does not follow the X-chip profile: on 6-22/23 it is 1080 ns on every chip while the copy halves. So the spatial profile is not local gas transport.

What varies along one axis only and per build: anything printed or laminated in stripes along the X lines (the resistive stripes run parallel to the X lines), or the X lines themselves (length to the connector, routing).

Sources: asym_more.py

The date and drift-field dependence collapse onto the cluster width

colour: drift voltage · filled: FEU 3 · open: FEU 7 · each point one sub-run

21

Details

Left, the drift time: at the same nominal 1000 V the pulses are ~1400 ns long on 6-22/23, 1140 on 6-18, 840 on 6-27/28 and 600 on 6-19, and the copy roughly orders the same way (0.17, 0.26, 0.10, 0.03; 6-18 and 6-22 swap). A longer pulse at fixed field means a slower drift: a different gas on different nights. But the drift time is not the variable: 6-23/24 at 600 V has shorter pulses than 6-22/23 and a larger copy.

For scale (Magboltz, 26.5 mm): at 1000 V the drift time is ~700 ns dry or with 1 % H2O; at 600 V it is 640 ns dry but 1220 ns with 1 % H2O; at 300 V 730 vs 3100 ns. The measured widths (shaping adds ~150–300 ns) follow the wet curve in the 6-27 scan. 6-22/23 needs an even slower gas at 1000 V.

Right, the cluster width: for Y-pad events the excess on n+1, in units of the Y pad’s own signal, falls on one curve against the Y ±1 share of the same events for all sessions and drift voltages: narrower clusters, larger copy. Wet Ar/iso diffuses less (D_T 0.024–0.031 vs 0.048 √cm dry) and its D_T changes with field, so both the gas of the night and the drift field set the width. Within one run, event by event, the width matters much less (only the widest fifth drops), so the width is a proxy for the gas state, not the mechanism itself.

6-19 has no Y in hand; its X ±1 share (0.84) would predict ~0.13 on this curve, against 0.03 measured. It stays an outlier: the night det3’s drift HV was sparking.

Also: the median amplitude drops at low drift field (6-27: 2080 ADC at 1000 V, 630 at 100 V): attachment, so the gas was not clean either.

Sources: asym_more.py, design/gas/*.json

Your gas-circulation idea, tested: not the cause, but the gas sets the size

what a flow pattern inside the chamber predicts, against what the data show

A gas-flow asymmetry predicts…Observed
Electrons are carried by the flowFlow ~mm/s against drift ~4 cm/µs: a 10⁻⁷ mm push.✗
A gain or composition gradientNeeds ~20 % change per 1.5 mm; compounded over 40 cm that is e⁵⁰.✗
It would act on X and Y alikeY has no copy (|a| ≲ 0.02) on every board.✗
A map following inlet → exhaustFlat top-to-bottom; changes along one axis only.✗
It should fade as the gas equalisesOn, off, on (6-18, 6-19, 6-22) and reversible with the drift field.✗
A large-scale causeThe same at every Y pad, absent over X pads.✗
The gas composition as a modulatorThe size follows the cluster width (diffusion), session to session.✓

What survives: the copy is a fixed, pad-level property of the board whose size is set by the gas transport (drift velocity, diffusion). A wetter or dirtier gas on some nights is the simplest reading.

22

Details

Why flow cannot do it: a few litres per hour through a ~5 L chamber is ~0.1–1 mm/s; electrons cross the 26.5 mm gap in ~1 µs. A composition gradient changes gain and drift velocity smoothly over centimetres; the copy needs a 20 % difference between strips 1.6 mm apart, the same at every Y pad, and only in X.

Equalisation: if the copy came from incoming gas mixing in, it would fall monotonically after a flush. Instead it was 0.26 on 6-18, 0.03 on 6-19, 0.16 on 6-22 and moves up and down with the drift voltage within an hour.

What to look for if the gas matters as a modulator: the copy should follow anything that changes the water or air content (flow rate, bottle change, lines opened, room humidity, how long the chamber sat unflushed).

Sources: NB_ASYM.md, asym_more.py

23

Details

No bench run scanned the drift field of any board but det3 (6-27; the 6-26 FEU-3 scan is empty on EOS). The beam ran drift × mesh scans on all four chambers: runs 58, 61, 64 (Ar/iso 90/10, 150–700 V), 12 (Ar/CF4/iso), 14/15/18/19 (95/5, 400–800 V), 3/5 (Ar/CO2). Extracted on condor (4502894) with raw_asym.py --cm.

Limits: the gamma flash needs the common-mode subtraction (it reads ~15–20 % lower than the raw bench extraction), beam gains are low (median 130–330 ADC), tracks come at an angle from the target (that shifts the X asymmetry: det2 reads ≈ 0 on the bench), and runs 3/12/14/15 used PS-only triggers or 20 ns sampling and gave no isolated tracks.

What it does say: in 90/10 the det3 copy does not grow at low drift field. Consistent with the bench reading that the driver is the gas transport (drift velocity and diffusion behave differently in 90/10), not the field itself.

What the simulations exclude: no static geometry makes it

3D weighting-field solves (bus_wpot.py, bus_float.py) + a forward model on uniform clouds with the data’s own estimator

geometryY-pad, σ 300X-pad, σ 300Y-pad, σ 450X-pad, σ 450
pads and vias only (symmetric)+0.007+0.003-0.011-0.000
one-sided bus, nominal depth+0.003+0.002-0.014-0.001
bus touching the pads (15 µm)-0.011+0.013-0.020+0.022

stripes floating, offset +200 µm-0.062-0.069-0.114-0.140

The copper alone (any bus depth, wet gap fill, kapton ε) gives |a| < 0.02 on the data’s estimator.

Floating stripes do make a real copy, but in both pad classes and growing with cloud size: the wrong fingerprint.

24

Details

Why the old 0.010 is not the data’s number: the old solve took the asymmetry of one channel’s kernel. The data pick the peak channel per event; a kernel that is only lopsided (the bus) is then absorbed by relabelling, and the forward model returns ~0. A copy that survives the peak selection needs line n+1 to receive a share of line n’s own signal.

Displacing the charge over Y pads also averages away (it only moves where the charge lands). Floating stripes (fast transverse equalisation, ~26 ns at 2 MΩ/sq) offset from the rows give 0.06–0.15, but equally for X- and Y-pad events and more for wider clouds; the data are the opposite on both counts.

Static dielectric variants (bus_wpot.py --eps-gap 20/80, --eps-kap 10): a wet gap fill lowers the bus pickup, the kapton permittivity hardly matters.

Sources: bus_wpot.py, bus_float.py, fwd_parity.py, fwd_out/*.json, bus_par/*.json

Strip or kapton gap? The resistive stripes leave no mark

det3 June-15 · true pad columns (each 64-ch connector reversed) · 39 stripes on 40 columns: the stripe slides 20 µm per column

Over the full beat the copy is flat: sine amplitude 0.007 ± 0.004 on 0.22. A stripe-mediated coupling (gold) would swing by ±0.1.

Which one a given event hit, stripe or gap, can’t be told: the cloud (σ ≈ 450 µm) covers more than one 800 µm period, and the peak pad fixes x only to ±390 µm.

25

Details

Geometry: ESL stripes 550 µm wide with 250 µm kapton gaps, 800 µm pitch, running along y; pads 680 µm on 780 µm. Pad column k sits at stripe phase (k·780 + x0) mod 800, so 40 columns sweep the stripe once under every pad. The column phase is exact per pad, so this tests every mechanism tied to how the stripes sit over the pads (a stripe over the Y pad vs over the gap next to it, a stripe over the bus gap, a floating stripe).

The earlier “no 40-channel period” check binned DAQ channel numbers, which are reversed inside each 64-channel connector and so mix the phases between connectors. Redone with true columns: Y-pad class sine amplitude 0.007 ± 0.004, X-pad class 0.006 ± 0.009; Y share 0.007 ± 0.005. det3 May and det2 are flat as well. Not even the sharing shows the stripes.

Why the per-event question has no handle: the charge cloud of a cosmic track has σ ≈ 450 µm (the forward model matches the data’s Y share 0.65 at σ 450), and inside the peak pad the landing point is uniform over ±390 µm, about one stripe period. The 800 µm harmonic is attenuated by exp(−2π²σ²/P²) ≈ 0.002 and again by the pad window. Every event covers stripes and gaps in about the 550:250 ratio. A per-event test needs a point source and short drift (collimated Fe-55, or X-rays converting near the mesh).

Sources: ../../2026-10-20/esl_cache.py, ../../2026-10-20/esl_bins.py, ../../2026-10-20/esl_share.py, ../../2026-10-20/esl_phase.py, fwd_out/f_off*.json

Caution: a plain channel copy also makes a parity split

Copy-free boards with x(n+1) += a·x(n) injected into the raw windows, then the identical peak + parity analysis

Y-pad class

X-pad class

Inject 0.3 into det2: 0.20 for Y-pad events, 0.05 for X-pad ones. Most of the 0.22 / 0.02 contrast is what peak selection does to any copy.

So the split alone does not show that the effect knows the pad type, or rule out electronics. The noise test still does. Closure: inject 0.3 into det2, undo 0.3 → -0.002 / +0.001.

26

Details

Why: when the copy lifts channel n+1 above n, the peak moves to n+1, the parity flips, and the event lands in the other class with a large negative asymmetry (its old centre is now at n−1). Y-pad events have an X central that is barely larger than its neighbours (the X pads all sit 780 µm from the charge), so they migrate most. The X-pad class collects the migrants and its mean is pulled down; the Y-pad class keeps the events where the copy stayed below the central.

The earlier control (forward model, symmetric geometry → 0 in both classes) only showed that the classification creates no asymmetry from nothing. It did not test what it does to a copy that is there. This injection does.

det4 and det7 (0.08 / 0.01 in the two classes) are consistent with a plain copy of a ≈ 0.15–0.20: undoing 0.20 leaves −0.01 / −0.06 and −0.02 / −0.04 (±0.02). For them the “Y-pad only” reading is not established.

Sources: ../../2026-10-20/inject_parity.py, ../../2026-10-20/uncopy_parity.py

det3 is not a plain copy: its X-pad events flip sign with cluster width

det3 June-15 by Y share, against a copy-free board with a plain copy injected

det3 June-15, Y-pad class

det3 June-15, X-pad class

det2 + plain copy 0.3, Y-pad

det2 + plain copy 0.3, X-pad

forward model, X offset 200 µm + copy 0.1, X-pad

Narrow clusters filed as X-pad: −0.40. A plain copy gives ≈ 0 there at any a, and undoing one (a = 0.35) leaves -0.43.

These are Y-pad charges whose X peak sits one column toward n+1: 13 % of narrow clusters on det3, 4–5 % on det2/det1 even with a 0.3 copy.

Pattern fits better as the X view’s sensitivity shifted ~200 µm toward n+1 relative to the Y view (gold), plus a small copy.

27

Details

Inverse test (uncopy_parity.py): undo a single copy a on the raw windows, re-find the peak, redo the split. On injected controls this closes exactly (both classes and every bin → 0 at the injected a). On det3 June-15, a = 0.33 flattens the Y-pad class in every bin, but the narrow X-pad bins stay at −0.43, −0.32, −0.19 for every a from 0 to 0.35, and the wide X-pad bins go negative. No single copy describes both.

Two-copy fit (fit_two_copy.py, separate a for Y-pad and X-pad charge, templates det2/det3 May/det1 reweighted to det3’s Y-share spectrum): best a_Y 0.30–0.35, a_X 0.05–0.15, but χ² 230–380 for 21 bins. The narrow X-pad bins stay at −0.07 … +0.05 against −0.40, whatever a_X is.

Migration (migrate.py): among clusters with Y share < 0.4, the X peak sits on the X-pad parity in 13.4 % of det3 June-15 events, 77 % of them with the larger neighbour at n−1 (the true Y-pad column). det2 and det1 give 4.0–4.5 % at a = 0–0.3 and need a ≈ 0.8 to reach 13 %. Caveat: det3 May (same PCB design) has a 20 % baseline here, so this number alone is not decisive. The −0.40 bin is.

Forward model (fwd_variants.py, solved weighting fields): a plain copy gives X-pad bins ≈ 0 → +0.2; an X-sensitivity offset of 200 µm toward n+1 gives −0.39 → +0.21, as in the data; offset + copy 0.1 also lifts the Y-pad class (+0.25 → −0.07, data +0.26 → +0.09). The model’s pad-type purity vs Y share is lower than the data’s (0.53–0.65 vs 0.87 in the narrowest bin), so only the shape is compared, not a χ².

Sources: ../../2026-10-20/uncopy_parity.py, ../../2026-10-20/inject_parity.py, ../../2026-10-20/fit_two_copy.py, ../../2026-10-20/migrate.py, ../../2026-10-20/fwd_variants.py

Not the one-sided readout (M1 cards, connectors, cables)

Anything after the pads is a fixed channel-to-channel mixing: it cannot know where the hit is, and it steps where the cards do

templateχ² no mixbest m(−1,+1,−2,+2)χ² bestnarrow X-pad
det24792+0.3, -0.1, -0.2, -0.2752 / 28-0.10 -0.19
det3 May1956+0.2, -0.1, -0.1, -0.1465 / 28+0.11 +0.12
det12514+0.3, -0.1, -0.2, -0.2410 / 28+0.23 +0.04
det3 June-15 data-0.40 -0.29

No linear mixing of neighbours, of any sign, makes the narrow X-pad bins negative while keeping the shares: −0.10 … +0.23 against −0.40 / −0.29.

Steps at connector edges rms 0.026, steps between bins inside a connector 0.041: no card boundaries in the profile.

Along the X line (distance from the readout edge, by Y chip): 0.21–0.27, flat. Coupling along the line or in the fan-out would grow with it.

29

Details

Every X line is read out at the same board edge, so the readout is not handed in x: line n and its two neighbours are read the same way. A passive coupling between neighbouring traces (fan-out, M1 card, cable) is reciprocal: it raises both neighbours and creates no left/right asymmetry, unless the routing order differs from the pad order. Any such effect, and any electronics effect, is a fixed linear map from channels to channels.

Test (mix_fit.py, mix_reach2.py): inject x′(n) = x(n) + Σ m_k x(n+k), k = ±1, ±2, negative values allowed (a derivative-like mixing that the noise test is blind to at first order), into copy-free boards, run det3’s full analysis, and score class asymmetries and ±1 sums in seven Y-share bins (the class fraction is left out: it differs between boards with no mixing). Grid m₋₁ 0–1, m₊₁ −0.5–0.5, m±₂ −0.2–0.2. The best mixing still leaves χ² 410–750 / 28, and the narrow X-pad bins never go below −0.19. The mixings that get there (m₋₁ ≈ 1) wreck the shares.

The reason is structural: det3 behaves as if the X view sensed the charge displaced relative to the Y pads. That is a change in the X–Y registration, and nothing acting on the X channels alone can make it.

The DAQ-neighbour pairs across a connector edge are tested directly on the next slide (re-extraction with chip-edge peaks kept). det4/det7 are consistent with a plain copy, so for them the readout question rests on that slide, the smooth profile and the noise test.

Sources: ../../2026-10-20/m1_profile.py, ../../2026-10-20/mix_fit.py, ../../2026-10-20/mix_reach2.py

The copy crosses connector boundaries with the pads, not with the electronics

Peaks at the edge of a 64-channel connector · re-extracted in true column order (raw_asym.py --edge)

det3 June-15, 6-23 (FEU 3)

det3 June-15, 6-28 (FEU 7)

det2

det3 May

det4

det3 6-23: when col−1 is on the other connector, cable and DREAM chip, it still gets the excess: +0.21 ± 0.03, as inside a connector.

Its DAQ n+1 there (same FEU, next chip, 127 columns away) gets α = 0.00. A copy made after the pads would land on DAQ n+1.

30

Details

Wiring: inside each 64-channel connector the DAQ order runs opposite to the columns, so DAQ n+1 is the next-lower column, except at the connector’s lowest column, where DAQ n+1 is the far (highest) column of the next connector and the physical neighbour col−1 is on the previous connector. The two orders separate there.

Extraction: peak search and the isolation cut (all channels over 5σ within ±3 columns) in column order, peaks with col mod 64 in 0..3 or 60..63; both the column-order and the DAQ-order 9-channel windows are stored. The usual good-pulse cut and hot-channel veto.

The 6-28 weekend run (FEU 7, copy ~0.09 inside) reads +0.03 ± 0.03 at the lowest column, 2σ below its inside value: not decisive alone. At col mod 64 = 63 (col+1 on the other connector) every board, controls included, reads +0.04 … +0.14: the cross-connector neighbour comes out low on all of them, a chip-to-chip or edge-pad effect common to the readout, which is why the clean comparison is the col mod 64 = 0 case.

Sources: asym_deck/raw_asym.py --edge, ../../2026-10-20/edge_test.py, edge_test.json

Details

Bins are Y-share quantiles in data and model separately, because the model’s Y-share scale and pad-type purity differ from the data’s (the static weighting fields have no resistive spreading and no shaping). Same night, 6-27: 1000 V drift gives −100 µm, 100–500 V gives −250 µm, reversibly. With quantile bins the absolute width is not used, so a fixed sensitivity extension whose effect grows for narrower clouds would show up here as an offset that grows with narrowness. That is what is seen; it is not yet evidence of a field-dependent geometry.

The bus traces sit on the side that gets the copy, but copper alone gives 1 %

Left: the pad/bus layout from the gerbers · right: copy from a 3D weighting-field solve vs data (log scale)

Even with the bus touching the pads the solve stays below det3’s copy, and a layout cannot vary across the board or with the field.

33

Details

Each X channel is every other pad along a line; its pads reach a bus line through 390 µm stubs that all point the same way, so the bus lies under the gap on one side of the channel’s own pads, next to one neighbour. Charge landing near that gap induces a little on the bus too: a one-sided, prompt, linear copy. The pad kernels used in the simulation drive the pads only, so they are symmetric by construction.

The solve (bus_wpot.py): own pads, vias, rings, stubs and bus at 1 V, everything else grounded, read at the resistive layer and folded with a 300–450 µm cloud. With the Geant4 stack estimate (264 µm FR4 per layer) it gives 0.010, about what det1/det2/det6 show. It reaches 0.085 only with the bus 15 µm below the pads, which no 8-layer board has.

Direction, checked 10-20: the column buses (DAQ X) are on the shallower bus layer (physical L5, L3-TrackY.gbr), the row buses (DAQ Y) on L6, which matches the copy being in X only (solve: L6 view ~0.001). In the gerbers the column buses fan out at the top and the row buses on the right; the detector has X connectors at the bottom and Y on the right seen from the pad side, so the gerber is that view mirrored in y, x kept. Every X stub runs +0.39 mm in x, so column c’s bus lies in the gap toward column c+1, beside the Y pads of column c+1. Charge on a Y pad therefore reaches the bus of the X line one column lower, which is DAQ n+1 after the connector reversal: the side that gets the copy. This relies on the ActiveAreaFrame / Mx17StripMap conventions (settled 2026-08-08).

So the bus is the one x-handed structure, on the right side, in the right view, and an extended one-sided sensitivity is what the forward model wants (slide “Not a copy”). What is missing is a factor ~20 in strength on the June-15 build (~6 on det4/det7), with the other boards at the copper value.

Sources: ../bus_wpot.py, ../bus_scan/d10_*.json, ../gerber_stubs.py

Every June board carries a smooth X field; det2’s bands cancel, det3’s does not (-74 µm)

Where the 3-strip X centroid is pulled by the n±1 asymmetry, per 8×8 cell of the board, matched X/Y cosmics

Raw survey, all bench sessions per board; colour clipped at ±160 µm

34

Details

dx = −(α₊₁ − α₋₁)/(1 + α₊₁ + α₋₁) × 780 µm along the true column axis (= +x in the wft frame: pos = 0.78 mm × true column on both views), α the in-phase content of the DAQ ±1 channels. Minus the symmetric reference (det3 May + det1, -0.7 µm). Cells with fewer than 25 events are grey.

Fixed geometry, variable size: one det3 map times one scale per session fits every session: 6-22/23 1000V ×0.96 (χ² 47/60), 6-23/24 600V ×1.57 (χ² 126/61), 6-27/28 1000V ×0.44 (χ² 47/59). The size follows the cloud width (gas, drift field).

det2: mean -1.6 µm but ±70 µm locally, in bands along y; that is why det2 looked like a clean control. det4/det6/det7 show fields too but have too few bench events for a cell map (13, 26 and 9 cells).

Sources: r5/corr_maps.py, r5/corr_maps.json, r5/map_fit.py (the registration-field fits)

Stripe registration makes the asymmetry in the sim, with both signs, at ~1/3 of the size

The sim’s 800 µm stripes slide 20 µm per 780 µm column, so each column has its own offset δ

sim, all X-only events

sim, narrow-cloud half

data range

A stripe sitting off the pad column’s centre registers the landed charge toward one neighbour. The data then need a print whose offset drifts across the board.

That needs a 780 µm-commensurate stripe pitch, against the 800 µm quote: the mask will tell.

35

Details

δ = signed distance from the peak column’s centre to the nearest stripe centre in the sim geometry (stripes at k·800 µm, columns at PAD_ORIGIN + c·780 µm). X-only events of the xo0 arms (th00 + thy*, seeds 5–16).

At δ = +150…+350 the sim also reproduces det3’s pad-class pattern (narrow-cloud X-pad events negative, wide positive); δ = −350…−150 gives the mirror, like det2’s negative bands. A rotation alone cannot make this: it only shortens the moiré.

Sources: r5/sim_delta.py, r5/sim_delta.json, FINDINGS.md sixth round

Details

Production slice: G_X of greens_comb_w2_rho5M_dk50um_g19um.npz at 9 times (sliced on lxplus). Variants: X-box W2 solves with conducting gaps (σ_gap = f·σ_strip, --gap-frac) or another strip width (--esl-width-um; 410/690 µm are 420/700 µm effective on the 20 µm grid), insulating otherwise. The nx = 1560 f = 0 control reproduces the production slice (0.024 at 300 ns).

Wide clouds (σ 450 µm) stay below 0.004 in every variant: the kernel effect is a narrow-cloud one, as in the data. Lower ρ_s only makes it arrive sooner (saturated by 92 ns at 0.5 MΩ/sq), never larger. Too much leak (f = 0.3) makes the sheet uniform and kills it.

Sources: r5/kernel_delta.py, response/solver/w2_production.py (family --nx --gap-frac --esl-width-um, combine-x), 2026-10-21/run_gx_gap.sh, condor 4520685, 4520736

The kernel’s late gain from a leak never reaches the peak-sample a1.

Width and funnelling act at the peak, but they don’t multiply: narrow gaps leave little to funnel.

37

Details

Baselines: funnel arms against the production-kernel D = 0 arms (condor 4507242); hybrid-kernel arms (production Y + nx = 1560 X kernels, 2026-10-21/build_hybrid.py) against the f = 0 hybrid control glg0 (×0.95 of the production arms: the grid). Error bars from the spread of the per-(angle, seed) paired differences.

Funnel: --gap-funnel F moves a fraction F of the avalanches that land in an ESL gap onto the nearer strip edge (20 µm inside) before the kernel lookup, with its own rng stream so the pairing is exact.

All arms are at 5 MΩ/sq. The 0.5 MΩ/sq arms (condor 4520942) test whether a faster sheet changes the timing.

Sources: r5/paired_odd.py, r5/paired_odd_*.json, condor 4520688, 4520810, 4520870, 4520871

39

Details

Over all angles the same estimator gives −14 ns on det3. The nTof_x17 study (sps_beam_test_26/analysis/cloud_basics/FINDINGS.md §42) selects tan ≈ −0.005 and reads +114 ns.

A late excess for vertical tracks is what sheet transport predicts (charge spreading across its stripe onto the neighbouring pad). The sim’s registration excess never comes out late, at any width or in any variant (funnel −110…−130 ns, wide stripes −101…−129 ns).

Sources: r5/timing_width.py, r5/timing_width.json, r5/delta_timing.py

40

Details

Frame: pos_mm = 0.78 × true column on both views of every board (read from the bench-cache windows), so the raw maps’ cells are the reco frame’s 49.92 mm cells with no flips. K is negative: the forward-model fit is pulled the opposite way to the 3-strip centroid, at ~80 % of its size.

Correction x − K·dx·scale with K from the other runs (leave-one-out); offset and rotation removed, which is what the alignment absorbs (it has no x-scale term). det2 136 → 108 and 34 → 23; det3 111 → 96, 99 → 94, 97 → 92; det4 worse (162 → 174) and det6/7 unchanged: their maps are too sparse, so they are excluded.

Shipped opt-in in nTof_x17: wft/xasym.py (correct_x(x_p0, y_p0, build, scale), a new column, no product changes), maps in wft/xasym_maps.json, tests wft/tests/test_xasym.py. Using it needs a re-alignment on corrected positions and the run’s scale.

Sources: 2026-10-21/reco_resid_map.py, reco_transfer.py, reco_correct_test.py, chpos_lookup.json

What it is: a fixed, smooth, two-signed X-only field on every June board, scaled by the cloud width. It is charge moved n−1 → n+1, locked to the pad pitch.

What is missing: the last factor in size, and the timing: late for vertical tracks in the data, always early in the sim.

For the analysis now: the production X position carries the field (K ≈ −0.8 of the centroid bias); wft.xasym corrects det2 and det3 June-15 (opt-in, new column, re-align after).

41

Details

Ledger of all 37 routes with verdicts: FINDINGS.md top. Rounds 4–8 here: X-offset sims, stripe direction per board, bookkeeping (moved, not added), the board fields, sim a1(δ), the kernel’s time build-up, the gap-leak, width and funnel arms, the timing split by width, and the transfer into the reconstruction.

what is open, and what would settle it

The June print sets it; the mask decides the pitch, the width and the offsets

Open

· Size: the best sim is ×1.6–1.8; the data need ×2.5–5.

· Timing: late for vertical tracks in data, early in every sim variant.

· The pitch: registration needs a 780 µm-commensurate print, the quote says 800.

· Why only the June builds: their gaps conduct (shown), and their print?

Next

1. The mask: stripe pitch, width and alignment, June vs May. Predict δ(x, y) per board.

2. Low-ρ_s arms (running): does a faster sheet make the excess late and keep its size?

3. For the analysis: wft.xasym on det2 and det3 June-15, with a re-alignment.

4. The det3 residual maps keep an x-scale term the alignment doesn’t fit.
